mcqs.q: Why is the integral term included in a PID controller?
options: To predict future errors based on rate of change
To eliminate steady-state error by accumulating past error values
To magnify the error signal for faster initial response
To reduce the sensitivity of the system to high-frequency sensor noise
mcqs.why: The integral term sums past errors to drive the residual, long-term difference (steady-state error) to zero.

mcqs.q: In which scenario would a designer likely choose a PI controller over a full PID controller?
options: When the process requires extremely fast anticipation of error changes
When the system is inherently unstable without derivative action
When measurement noise is significant and derivative action would cause instability
When there is absolutely no steady-state error present in the system
mcqs.why: Derivative action is highly sensitive to noise in the measurement signal, so it is often omitted in noisy environments.

mcqs.q: Which is true regarding the relationship between control gain and system stability?
options: Higher gain always improves stability without exception
Excessive gain can cause a system to oscillate or diverge
Lower gain always results in faster settling times
Gain has no effect on the stability of a control loop
mcqs.why: While gain increases responsiveness, excessive gain effectively amplifies errors to the point where the system becomes unstable and oscillates.

definitions.16: A group of interconnected electrical or mechanical components arranged to perform a specific signal processing or control function.
definitions.17: A hybrid network combining both phase lead and phase lag characteristics to simultaneously improve system stability and steady-state accuracy.
definitions.18: A specific representation of a transfer function as the ratio of output to input current or voltage across a network.
definitions.19: The argument of a complex transfer function, representing the phase shift introduced by a network to an input signal at a given frequency.

mcqs.q: Why is a lead-lag compensator used instead of just a lead or lag compensator in some control systems?
options: To simultaneously improve both transient response and steady-state error
To reduce the overall cost of the control system hardware
To eliminate the need for a transfer function analysis
To simplify the root locus plot for analysis
mcqs.why: A lead-lag compensator combines the high-frequency phase lead of a lead network with the low-frequency phase lag of a lag network.

mcqs.q: What is the primary effect of adding a lag compensator to a control system?
options: It increases the system's stability margin significantly
It reduces the steady-state error for low-frequency inputs
It increases the system's bandwidth and speed
It eliminates all resonant peaks in the frequency response
mcqs.why: Lag compensators provide phase lag at low frequencies, which increases the system gain at low frequencies, reducing steady-state error.

mcqs.q: In the context of a lead-lag compensator, what do the poles and zeros represent in the transfer function?
options: The physical locations of components on a circuit board
The frequencies where the system's output and input are equal
The values of the complex variable s where the numerator and denominator are zero
The specific values of the input signal that cause instability
mcqs.why: Poles and zeros are the roots of the denominator and numerator polynomials of the transfer function, respectively, defining the system's dynamic behavior.

mcqs.q: Why does an induction motor develop torque only when there is slip between the stator field and rotor?
options: Because Lenz's Law requires relative motion to induce a current
Because the rotor must be connected to an external DC source
Because synchronous speed produces a constant magnetic field
Because the stator field rotates only at zero slip
mcqs.why: Torque requires induced rotor current, which only exists when there is relative motion (slip) to induce it.

mcqs.q: What is the primary reason a standard single-phase induction motor cannot start on its own?
options: It produces two equal and opposite counter-rotating magnetic fields
Its rotor bars are too heavy to accelerate
The stator field is stationary at zero frequency
Lenz's Law prevents any initial torque
mcqs.why: The opposing fields create zero net starting torque, requiring auxiliary starting methods.

mcqs.q: If a three-phase motor has 6 poles and operates at 50 Hz, what is its synchronous speed in RPM?
options: 1500 RPM
1000 RPM
3000 RPM
2000 RPM
mcqs.why: Synchronous speed equals (120 x frequency)/poles = (120 x 50)/6 = 1000 RPM.

candidates.label: Electric power distribution
candidates.context: Electric power distribution is the final stage in the delivery of electricity.

candidates.label: Electric power
candidates.context: The problem of transmitting electricity over longer distances became a recognized engineering roadblock to electric power distribution, with many less-than-satisfactory solutions tested by lighting companies.

candidates.label: Medium voltage
candidates.context: Primary distribution lines carry this medium voltage power to distribution transformers located near the customer's premises.

candidates.label: Distribution lines
candidates.context: Primary distribution lines carry this medium voltage power to distribution transformers located near the customer's premises.

candidates.label: Distribution transformer
candidates.context: Distribution transformers again lower the voltage to the utilization voltage used by lighting, industrial equipment and household appliances.

candidates.label: Distribution voltages
candidates.context: Primary distribution voltages range from 4 kV to 35 kV phase-to-phase (2.4 kV to 20 kV phase-to-neutral) Only large consumers are fed directly from distribution voltages; most utility customers are connected to a transformer, which reduces the distribution voltage to the low voltage "utilization voltage", "supply voltage" or "mains voltage" used by lighting and interior wiring systems.

candidates.label: United States
candidates.context: Closer to the customer, a distribution transformer steps the primary distribution power down to a low-voltage secondary circuit, usually 120/240 V in the United States for residential customers.

candidates.label: Power station
candidates.context: Electric power distribution become necessary only in the 1880s, when electricity started being generated at power stations.

candidates.label: Alternating-current (AC)
candidates.context: Compared to direct current, AC had much lower transmission costs and greater economies of scale—with large AC generating plants capable of supplying entire cities and regions leading to the rapid introduction of AC.

candidates.label: Direct-current (DC)
candidates.context: For example, Hydro-Québec has a direct-current line which goes from the James Bay region to Boston.

candidates.label: Distribution system
candidates.context: Traditionally, the distribution systems would only operate as simple distribution lines where the electricity from the transmission networks would be shared among the customers.

candidates.label: Arc lighting
candidates.context: The high voltages used in arc lighting allowed a single generating station to supply a string of lights up to 7 miles (11 km) long.

candidates.label: Incandescent lighting
candidates.context: By contrast, direct-current indoor incandescent lighting systems, such as Edison's first power station, installed in 1882, had difficulty supplying customers more than a mile away because they used a low voltage (110 V) from generation to end use.

candidates.label: Lighting running
candidates.context: The first power-distribution systems installed in European and US cities were used to supply lighting: arc lighting running on very-high-voltage (around 3,000 V) alternating current (AC) or direct current (DC), and incandescent lighting running on low-voltage (100 V) direct current.

candidates.label: Lighting systems
candidates.context: Both were supplanting gas lighting systems, with arc lighting taking over large-area and street lighting, and incandescent lighting replacing gas lights for business and residential users.

candidates.label: Generating station
candidates.context: Electric power begins at a generating station, where the potential difference can be as high as 33,000 volts.

candidates.label: Longer distances
candidates.context: The problem of transmitting electricity over longer distances became a recognized engineering roadblock to electric power distribution, with many less-than-satisfactory solutions tested by lighting companies.

candidates.label: Electric motor
candidates.context: AC became the dominant form of transmission of power with innovations in Europe and the US in electric motor designs, and the development of engineered universal systems allowing the large number of legacy systems to be connected to large AC grids.

candidates.label: Electrification systems
candidates.context: Rural electrification systems tend to use higher distribution voltages because of the longer distances covered by distribution lines (see Rural Electrification Administration).

candidates.label: Phase-to-phase
candidates.context: Primary distribution voltages range from 4 kV to 35 kV phase-to-phase (2.4 kV to 20 kV phase-to-neutral) Only large consumers are fed directly from distribution voltages; most utility customers are connected to a transformer, which reduces the distribution voltage to the low voltage "utilization voltage", "supply voltage" or "mains voltage" used by lighting and interior wiring systems.

candidates.label: Radial system

candidates.label: Distribution network

candidates.label: Source of supply

candidates.label: Trip savers

candidates.label: Single objective

candidates.label: Active power loss
candidates.context: Some authors have proposed Pareto optimality based approaches (including active power losses and reliability indices as objectives).

candidates.label: Rural electrification

candidates.label: Three-phase
candidates.context: Three-phase electric power is more efficient in terms of power delivered per cable used, and is more suited to running large electric motors.

candidates.label: Single-phase

candidates.label: Industrial customers

candidates.label: Split-phase
candidates.context: Most of the Americas use 60 Hz AC, the 120/240 volt split-phase system domestically and three phase for larger installations.

candidates.label: North American

candidates.label: Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM)
candidates.context: OFDM is a frequency-division multiplexing (FDM) scheme that was introduced by Robert W. Chang of Bell Labs in 1966.

candidates.label: Frequency-division multiplexing (FDM)
candidates.context: In telecommunications, orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) is a type of digital transmission used in digital modulation for encoding digital (binary) data on multiple carrier frequencies.

candidates.label: Guard interval
candidates.context: The guard interval also eliminates the need for a pulse-shaping filter, and it reduces the sensitivity to time synchronization problems.

candidates.label: Multipath propagation
candidates.context: OFDM was improved by Weinstein and Ebert in 1971 with the introduction of a guard interval, providing better orthogonality in transmission channels affected by multipath propagation.

candidates.label: Symbol rate
candidates.context: The low symbol rate makes the use of a guard interval between symbols affordable, making it possible to eliminate intersymbol interference (ISI) and use echoes and time-spreading (in analog television visible as ghosting and blurring, respectively) to achieve a diversity gain, i.e. a signal-to-noise ratio improvement.

candidates.label: Modulation scheme
candidates.context: Each subcarrier (signal) is modulated with a conventional modulation scheme (such as quadrature amplitude modulation or phase-shift keying) at a low symbol rate.

candidates.label: Channel conditions
candidates.context: The effects of frequency-selective channel conditions, for example fading caused by multipath propagation, can be considered as constant (flat) over an OFDM sub-channel if the sub-channel is sufficiently narrow-banded (i.e., if the number of sub-channels is sufficiently large).

candidates.label: Intersymbol interference
candidates.context: Intersymbol interference can be avoided if the multipath time-spreading (the time between the reception of the first and the last echo) is shorter than the guard interval (i.e., 125 microseconds).

candidates.label: Single frequency network (SFN)
candidates.context: A single frequency network is a form of transmitter macrodiversity.

candidates.label: Coded orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing
candidates.context: In coded orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (COFDM), forward error correction (convolutional coding) and time/frequency interleaving are applied to the signal being transmitted.

candidates.label: Error correction
candidates.context: OFDM is invariably used in conjunction with channel coding (forward error correction), and almost always uses frequency and/or time interleaving.

candidates.label: Frequency interleaving
candidates.context: Usually, additional interleaving (on top of the time and frequency interleaving mentioned above) in between the two layers of coding is implemented.

candidates.label: Long-Term Evolution (LTE)
candidates.context: 5G NR is the successor to LTE. the now defunct Qualcomm/3GPP2 Ultra Mobile Broadband (UMB) project, intended as a successor of CDMA2000, but replaced by LTE.

candidates.label: Orthogonal frequency-division multiple access
candidates.context: OFDMA is also a candidate access method for the IEEE 802.22 Wireless Regional Area Networks (WRAN).

candidates.label: Mobile broadband wireless access (MBWA)
candidates.context: OFDMA is used in: the mobility mode of the IEEE 802.16 Wireless MAN standard, commonly referred to as WiMAX, the IEEE 802.20 mobile Wireless MAN standard, commonly referred to as MBWA, the 3GPP Long-Term Evolution (LTE) fourth generation mobile broadband standard downlink.

candidates.label: Multiple access
candidates.context: However, OFDM can be combined with multiple access using time, frequency or coding separation of the users.

candidates.label: OFDM-based
candidates.context: In OFDM-based wide-area broadcasting, receivers can benefit from receiving signals from several spatially dispersed transmitters simultaneously, since transmitters will only destructively interfere with each other on a limited number of subcarriers, whereas in general they will actually reinforce coverage over a wide area.

candidates.label: WiMAX
candidates.context: OFDMA is used in: the mobility mode of the IEEE 802.16 Wireless MAN standard, commonly referred to as WiMAX, the IEEE 802.20 mobile Wireless MAN standard, commonly referred to as MBWA, the 3GPP Long-Term Evolution (LTE) fourth generation mobile broadband standard downlink.

candidates.label: Evolved UMTS Terrestrial Radio Access (E-UTRA)
candidates.context: The radio interface was formerly named High Speed OFDM Packet Access (HSOPA), now named Evolved UMTS Terrestrial Radio Access (E-UTRA) WLAN IEEE 802.11ax DOCSIS 3.1 Upstream

candidates.label: High Speed OFDM Packet Access (HSOPA)
candidates.context: The radio interface was formerly named High Speed OFDM Packet Access (HSOPA), now named Evolved UMTS Terrestrial Radio Access (E-UTRA) WLAN IEEE 802.11ax DOCSIS 3.1 Upstream

candidates.label: Spectral efficiency
candidates.context: The orthogonality also allows high spectral efficiency, with a total symbol rate near the Nyquist rate for the equivalent baseband signal (i.e., near half the Nyquist rate for the double-side band physical passband signal).

candidates.label: Sub-channel
candidates.context: The effects of frequency-selective channel conditions, for example fading caused by multipath propagation, can be considered as constant (flat) over an OFDM sub-channel if the sub-channel is sufficiently narrow-banded (i.e., if the number of sub-channels is sufficiently large).

candidates.label: Peak-to-average-power ratio (PAPR)
candidates.context: An OFDM signal exhibits a high peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) because the independent phases of the subcarriers mean that they will often combine constructively.

candidates.label: Cyclic prefix
candidates.context: The cyclic prefix, which is transmitted during the guard interval, consists of the end of the OFDM symbol copied into the guard interval, and the guard interval is transmitted followed by the OFDM symbol.

candidates.label: Doppler shift
candidates.context: While Doppler shift alone may be compensated for by the receiver, the situation is worsened when combined with multipath, as reflections will appear at various frequency offsets, which is much harder to correct.

candidates.label: Passband bandwidth
candidates.context: Therefore, with N subcarriers, the total passband bandwidth will be B ≈ N·Δf (Hz).

candidates.label: FFT
candidates.context: The orthogonality allows for efficient modulator and demodulator implementation using the FFT algorithm on the receiver side, and inverse FFT on the sender side.

candidates.label: Single-side band (SSB)
candidates.context: A single-side band (SSB) or vestigial sideband (VSB) modulation scheme would achieve almost half that bandwidth for the same symbol rate (i.e., twice as high spectral efficiency for the same symbol alphabet length).

candidates.label: Vestigial sideband (VSB)
candidates.context: A single-side band (SSB) or vestigial sideband (VSB) modulation scheme would achieve almost half that bandwidth for the same symbol rate (i.e., twice as high spectral efficiency for the same symbol alphabet length).

candidates.label: Inter-carrier interference (ICI)
candidates.context: OFDM requires very accurate frequency synchronization between the receiver and the transmitter; with frequency deviation the subcarriers will no longer be orthogonal, causing inter-carrier interference (ICI) (i.e., cross-talk between the subcarriers).

candidates.label: WCP-OFDM Weighted Cyclic Prefix
candidates.context: For example, a low-complexity scheme referred to as WCP-OFDM (Weighted Cyclic Prefix Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing) consists of using short filters at the transmitter output in order to perform a potentially non-rectangular pulse shaping and a near perfect reconstruction using a single-tap per subcarrier equalization.

candidates.label: FFT algorithm
candidates.context: The orthogonality allows for efficient modulator and demodulator implementation using the FFT algorithm on the receiver side, and inverse FFT on the sender side.

candidates.label: OFDM symbol
candidates.context: Since the duration of each symbol is long, it is feasible to insert a guard interval between the OFDM symbols, thus eliminating the intersymbol interference.

candidates.label: Channel coding
candidates.context: OFDM is invariably used in conjunction with channel coding (forward error correction), and almost always uses frequency and/or time interleaving.

candidates.label: Bit-stream
candidates.context: Similarly, time interleaving ensures that bits that are originally close together in the bit-stream are transmitted far apart in time, thus mitigating against severe fading as would happen when travelling at high speed.

candidates.label: Compact disc (CD)
candidates.context: A similar design of audio data encoding makes compact disc (CD) playback robust.

candidates.label: Reed-Solomon
candidates.context: The choice for Reed-Solomon coding as the outer error correction code is based on the observation that the Viterbi decoder used for inner convolutional decoding produces short error bursts when there is a high concentration of errors, and Reed-Solomon codes are inherently well suited to correcting bursts of errors.

candidates.label: Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN)
candidates.context: Examples of such error correction coding types include turbo codes and LDPC codes, which perform close to the Shannon limit for the Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) channel.

candidates.label: Discrete multitone modulation (DMT)
candidates.context: The term discrete multitone modulation (DMT) denotes OFDM-based communication systems that adapt the transmission to the channel conditions individually for each subcarrier, by means of so-called bit-loading.

candidates.label: Ultra Mobile Broadband (UMB)
candidates.context: 5G NR is the successor to LTE. the now defunct Qualcomm/3GPP2 Ultra Mobile Broadband (UMB) project, intended as a successor of CDMA2000, but replaced by LTE.

candidates.label: Wireless Regional Area Networks (WRAN)
candidates.context: OFDMA is also a candidate access method for the IEEE 802.22 Wireless Regional Area Networks (WRAN).

definitions.1: An integrated circuit (IC) is a set of electronic circuits on a small flat piece of semiconductor material, typically silicon, that integrates transistors, diodes, and other components.
definitions.2: A microprocessor is a multipurpose, clock-driven, register-based digital integrated circuit that accepts binary data, processes it per stored instructions, and outputs results.
definitions.3: A central processing unit (CPU) is the primary component of a computer that performs arithmetic, logic, control, and input/output operations according to stored programs.
definitions.4: Large-scale integration (LSI) is a level of integration in which hundreds of transistors are placed on a single chip, enabling more complex digital circuits.
definitions.5: Very-large-scale integration (VLSI) is a technology level for integrated circuits where thousands to millions of transistors are fabricated on a single chip.
definitions.6: Metal-oxide-semiconductor (MOS) is a fabrication technology for integrated circuits that uses a metal gate, an insulating oxide layer, and a semiconductor substrate to create transistors.
definitions.7: Single-chip refers to the design approach of integrating all the essential components of a computer processor onto one single integrated circuit.
definitions.8: Embedded systems are dedicated computing systems designed to perform specific control functions within a larger mechanical or electrical system.
definitions.11: A digital signal processor (DSP) is a specialized microprocessor designed to perform high-speed mathematical operations on digital signals.
definitions.12: An arithmetic logic unit (ALU) is the digital circuit within a processor that performs arithmetic and logical operations on binary data.
definitions.14: General-purpose refers to a processor designed to perform a wide variety of computing tasks rather than being limited to one specific function.
definitions.15: Graphics processing units (GPUs) are specialized processors designed primarily for the rapid manipulation and rendering of visual and geometric data.
definitions.16: An MOS chip is an integrated circuit fabricated using metal-oxide-semiconductor technology, which forms the basis of modern digital electronics.
definitions.18: MOS LSI chips are early integrated circuits that combined metal-oxide-semiconductor technology with large-scale integration, allowing hundreds of transistors on one chip.
definitions.20: Silicon-gate technology (SGT) is a MOS fabrication process that uses a silicon gate electrode instead of a metal gate, improving performance and density.
definitions.21: Fairchild Semiconductor was a pioneering American semiconductor company that developed early MOS and silicon-gate integrated circuits.
definitions.25: The Central Air Data Computer (CADC) was a specialized microprocessor developed by Garrett AiResearch for the US Navy F-14 Tomcat fighter jet.
definitions.31: The Four-Phase Systems AL1 was an early 8-bit bit-slice microprocessor chip designed by Lee Boysel in 1969, containing registers and an ALU.
definitions.32: RAM is random-access memory, a type of volatile computer memory that can be read and changed in any order, typically used for temporary data storage.
definitions.33: ROM is read-only memory, a type of non-volatile memory used in computers and other electronic devices to store firmware or permanent software.

mcqs.q: Why does integrating a whole CPU onto a single chip using VLSI greatly reduce the cost of computing?
options: It eliminates the need for any external memory components.
It allows for highly automated mass production of the core processing component on a single substrate.
It significantly increases the clock speed of the processor without adding power consumption.
It makes the processor capable of interpreting high-level programming languages directly.
mcqs.why: VLSI allows the entire CPU to be mass-produced on a single silicon wafer, drastically reducing per-unit manufacturing costs.

mcqs.q: What is the primary advantage of silicon-gate MOS technology over earlier metal-gate MOS?
options: It allows for the integration of analog components on the same chip.
It enables higher transistor density and better reliability by using a silicon gate electrode.
It completely eliminates the need for an insulating oxide layer in the transistor structure.
It reduces the word size of the processor to improve power efficiency.
mcqs.why: Silicon gates replaced metal gates to improve performance and integration density in MOS chips.

mcqs.q: In the context of embedded systems, why is a microprocessor control program often preferred over non-programmable controls?
options: It requires less physical space and can be easily tailored to fit specific product needs.
It operates at a significantly higher clock speed than non-programmable logic.
It eliminates the need for any hardware components like sensors or actuators.
It is always more power-efficient regardless of the specific software routine.
mcqs.why: Embedded software allows for flexible, tailored control and performance upgrades without redesigning the physical hardware.

mcqs.q: Why can processors with different microarchitectures run the same machine code?
options: Because the microarchitecture is defined by the operating system.
Because the ISA provides a stable, abstract interface for the machine code.
Because the ISA and microarchitecture are identical concepts.
Because the compiler translates machine code for each microarchitecture.
mcqs.why: ISA defines the abstract interface, enabling binary compatibility across different implementations.

mcqs.q: What is a key design goal of a Reduced instruction set computer (RISC) architecture?
options: To implement a large number of complex, specialized instructions.
To simplify the processor by efficiently implementing only frequently used instructions.
To rely heavily on elaborate instructions for complex operations.
To execute instructions sequentially without any control flow.
mcqs.why: RISC simplifies the processor by focusing on frequently used instructions, often implemented as subroutines.

mcqs.q: What is the primary function of operand specifiers in an instruction?
options: To specify the addressing modes for memory access.
To define the operation to be performed by the processor.
To specify the registers, memory locations, or data to be used in the operation.
To control the flow of execution through conditional branches.
mcqs.why: Operand specifiers identify the actual data or locations involved in the instruction's operation.

mcqs.q: Why is PC-relative addressing preferred for conditional jumps in modern architectures?

It allows for position-independent code and handles small jumps efficiently.
It is always faster than absolute addressing because it requires no registers.
It eliminates the need for a program counter entirely.
mcqs.why: PC-relative addressing calculates offsets relative to the current PC, enabling position-independent code and efficient short-range jumps.

To determine the specific operation (add, subtract) to be performed.
To define how the effective address of an operand is calculated.
To store the results of arithmetic operations in temporary memory.
mcqs.why: Addressing modes dictate the mathematical or logical steps required to derive the actual memory address where the required data resides.

mcqs.q: In register indirect addressing, where is the effective address of the operand located?

In the contents of a specific CPU register.

mcqs.q: What is the primary architectural advantage of Memory-mapped I/O over port-mapped I/O in modern processors?
options: It uses a separate dedicated bus for all I/O communication.
It allows the use of all general-purpose registers and standard memory instructions for I/O.
It eliminates the need for any address decoding hardware.
It prevents all cache coherency issues during data transfer.
mcqs.why: MMIO leverages standard memory instructions, making I/O operations more flexible.

mcqs.q: If a system uses 'incomplete' (partial) address decoding, what is the most likely result?
options: The system becomes significantly faster than with complete decoding.
The system cannot access any RAM above the first 64KB.
A single hardware register may be accessible via multiple different memory addresses.
The CPU cannot distinguish between RAM and I/O devices.
mcqs.why: Partial decoding ignores some address lines, causing multiple addresses to map to the same register.

mcqs.q: Why must developers be cautious when using caches with Memory-mapped I/O?
options: Caches are always too slow to access I/O devices.
Caches can reorder writes, potentially causing peripheral registers to be accessed in the wrong order.
Caches consume too much power when communicating with I/O devices.
Caches prevent direct memory access (DMA) from functioning.
mcqs.why: Cache reordering can violate the intended order of operations required by peripheral hardware.

candidates.label: Frequency response
candidates.context: The frequency response allows simpler analysis of cascaded systems such as multistage amplifiers, as the response of the overall system can be found through multiplication of the individual stages' frequency responses (as opposed to convolution of the impulse response in the time domain).

candidates.label: Mechanical vibration
candidates.context: In signal processing, electronics and mechanical vibration, the frequency response of a system is the quantitative measure of the magnitude and phase of the output as a function of input frequency.

candidates.label: Control systems
candidates.context: In control systems, such as a vehicle's cruise control, it may be used to assess system stability, often through the use of Bode plots.

candidates.label: Bode plot
candidates.context: In many frequency domain applications, the phase response is relatively unimportant, and the magnitude response of the Bode plot may be all that is required.

candidates.label: Impulse response
candidates.context: The frequency response characterizes systems in the frequency domain, just as the impulse response characterizes systems in the time domain.

candidates.label: Response characterizes systems
candidates.context: The frequency response characterizes systems in the frequency domain, just as the impulse response characterizes systems in the time domain.

candidates.label: Fourier transform
candidates.context: Measuring the frequency response typically involves exciting the system with an input signal and measuring the resulting output signal, calculating the frequency spectra of the two signals (for example, using the fast Fourier transform for discrete signals), and comparing the spectra to isolate the effect of the system.

candidates.label: Linear systems
candidates.context: In linear systems (or as an approximation to a real system, neglecting second-order non-linear properties), either response completely describes the system, and thus there is a one-to-one correspondence: the frequency response is the Fourier transform of the impulse response.

mcqs.q: Why is cycle stealing mode preferred over burst mode in certain systems?
options: It transfers data faster by using the entire bus continuously.
It allows the CPU to perform work between small data transfers.
It requires fewer hardware registers in the DMA controller.
It is simpler to implement in software without any special hardware.
mcqs.why: Cycle stealing is designed to interleave DMA transfers with CPU activity to avoid long idle periods.

mcqs.q: What problem occurs in a write-back cache when a device uses DMA to write to memory?
options: The CPU immediately receives an interrupt for every write operation.
The CPU might read a stale value from its cache that has not been updated in memory.
The DMA controller cannot access memory without flushing the entire cache.
The memory address register in the DMA controller becomes invalid.
mcqs.why: In a write-back cache, the CPU's cached copy is not updated in memory, leading to stale data.

mcqs.q: What must be ensured when a peripheral acts as a bus master in a system?
options: The CPU must be powered off during the entire transfer.
The peripheral must be connected directly to the main memory without a bus.
The processor must be put into a hold condition to prevent bus contention.
The DMA controller must use cycle stealing mode exclusively.
mcqs.why: Putting the CPU in a hold condition prevents bus contention when the peripheral takes control.

mcqs.q: Why were early ARM designs limited to a 26-bit address space rather than using the full 32-bit capacity of the register?
options: To allow the program counter and processor status flags to share a single 32-bit register.
Because 32-bit memory was significantly more expensive to manufacture in the 1980s.
The instruction set architecture required the extra bits for floating-point calculations.
Early ARM processors were specifically designed for 8-bit systems, which cannot support 32-bit addressing.
mcqs.why: The design allowed the PC (24 bits) and processor flags (8 bits) to fit into one 32-bit register, simplifying interrupt handling.

mcqs.q: What is the primary advantage of the 'Fast Interrupt reQuest' (FIQ) mode found in early ARM designs?
options: It eliminates the need for a memory controller.
It allows the CPU to run at double the clock speed during interrupts.
It uses dedicated registers to avoid saving the state, speeding up interrupt service routines.
It automatically upgrades the instruction set from 16-bit to 32-bit.
mcqs.why: FIQ mode improves performance by banking registers 8-14, which removes the overhead of saving the machine state during an interrupt.

mcqs.q: How does the ARM philosophy toward hardware-software interaction compare to traditional CISC architectures?
options: ARM relies solely on software to manage memory, whereas CISC uses hardware only.
ARM generally prefers simplicity in instructions, pushing more complex logic into software when possible.
ARM integrates all possible peripheral functions into the hardware to remove software dependency.
ARM designs are identical to CISC designs, just with a different marketing name.
mcqs.why: RISC architectures like ARM prioritize simple, single-cycle instructions and often leave complex tasks for software implementation.

definitions.15: Register write back is the final stage of a pipeline where the result of an operation is written to a destination register.
definitions.16: Instruction decode is the pipeline stage that translates the fetched instruction into control signals for subsequent execution.
definitions.17: Register fetch is the pipeline stage that reads operand values from source registers into the execution unit.
definitions.20: Branch prediction is a technique used by processors to guess the outcome of a conditional branch to avoid pipeline stalls.
definitions.21: A pipelined processor is a CPU that executes multiple instructions simultaneously by processing them in different pipeline stages.
definitions.22: Sequential execution is the assumption that one instruction must fully complete before the next one begins.
definitions.24: Delay slots are empty cycles in a pipeline where a processor executes unrelated instructions to fill the gap after a branch.
definitions.25: Operand forwarding is a hardware mechanism that routes a computed value directly to a dependent instruction before it is written to a register.
definitions.26: Out-of-order execution is an optimization where a processor executes instructions in an order different from their original program sequence.
definitions.31: A list of instructions is a sequence of machine-level commands that a processor fetches and processes.

A single bus must be shared to fetch both instructions and data, creating a throughput limit.
Memory capacity is too small to store large programs.
The control unit cannot sequence operations fast enough.

mcqs.q: Which scenario best describes a cache hit during a processor memory access operation?
options: The CPU finds the requested data address already stored in the cache memory.
The CPU successfully writes new data to the main memory via the cache.
The CPU fetches data from the main memory after a stall.
The cache evicts an old entry to make room for new data.
mcqs.why: A cache hit occurs specifically when the processor locates the required data within the cache.

mcqs.q: Why does a cache miss significantly impact processor performance?
options: It forces the CPU to switch to a different operating system.
It causes the CPU to stall while waiting for data from slower main memory.
It leads to the permanent deletion of data from the cache.
It increases the clock speed of the CPU uncontrollably.
mcqs.why: When data is not in the cache, the CPU must wait for the much slower main memory, causing a stall.

mcqs.q: What is the primary advantage of a set-associative cache design over a direct-mapped cache?
options: It eliminates the need for any replacement policy.
It allows a memory block to be placed in any cache line without restriction.
It reduces the probability of conflict misses by providing multiple slots per set.
It uses significantly less power because it does not require tags.
mcqs.why: Set-associative caches provide multiple locations for a block to reside, reducing conflicts compared to direct mapping.

mcqs.q: What was the primary design motivation behind the original CISC philosophy in the 1960s and 70s?
options: To minimize the power consumption of portable mobile devices
To simplify hardware design by removing complex addressing modes
To bridge the semantic gap between high-level language constructs and machine code
To maximize the speed of single-cycle instruction execution
mcqs.why: Architects aimed to make machine code closer to the complexity of high-level programming to improve productivity and code density.

mcqs.q: Why might a 'complex' instruction implemented via microcode actually decrease performance compared to a sequence of simple instructions?
options: Microcode is too simple to perform arithmetic operations.
It may include side effects or unnecessary hardware interactions that demand extra, inefficient clock cycles.
Microcode instructions require more memory space than hardwired logic.
It forces the compiler to ignore high-level language optimizations.
mcqs.why: Over-designed instructions can cause bottlenecks or unintended side effects, making them slower than an equivalent sequence of simple instructions.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a key advantage of the RISC approach compared to traditional CISC designs?
options: It allows for easier implementation of pipelining due to instruction regularity.
It uses complex variable-length instructions to save memory space.
It avoids the use of internal microcode entirely by using only external hardware.
It requires significantly more transistors than a CISC design.
mcqs.why: RISC's simplicity and fixed instruction length make overlapping stages (pipelining) much easier to manage than in variable-length CISC designs.

mcqs.q: What is the primary purpose of storing the key alongside the value in a hash table?

To handle collisions by verifying the correct key during lookup
To increase the speed of the hashing function
To eliminate the need for an associative array structure
mcqs.why: Storing the key is necessary because multiple keys might hash to the same index (collision), so one must verify the key to retrieve the correct value.

mcqs.q: Why does the performance of a hash table generally deteriorate as the load factor increases?
options: Because the hash function becomes less accurate
Because memory addresses become fragmented
Because collisions become more frequent, requiring more work to resolve
Because the computer cannot process large integer values
mcqs.why: A higher load factor means more entries occupy the limited number of buckets, increasing the probability of collisions and time spent searching.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a strict limitation of using open addressing in a hash table?

It cannot be used with integer keys
It requires a secondary linked list for every slot
It cannot support dynamic resizing
mcqs.why: In open addressing, each slot can only hold one item, so the load factor cannot exceed 1.0; the total elements cannot exceed the capacity.

candidates.context: Divide-and-conquer algorithms naturally tend to make efficient use of memory caches.

candidates.label: Sub-problem
candidates.context: The reason is that once a sub-problem is small enough, it and all its sub-problems can, in principle, be solved within the cache, without accessing the slower main memory.

candidates.label: fast Fourier transform (FFT)
candidates.context: An early example of a divide-and-conquer algorithm with multiple subproblems is Gauss's 1805 description of what is now called the Cooley–Tukey fast Fourier transform (FFT) algorithm, although he did not analyze its operation count quantitatively, and FFTs did not become widespread until they were rediscovered over a century later.

candidates.label: Solving
candidates.context: Divide and conquer is a powerful tool for solving conceptually difficult problems: all it requires is a way of breaking the problem into sub-problems, of solving the trivial cases, and of combining sub-problems to the original problem.

candidates.label: Mathematical induction

candidates.label: Divide-and-conquer paradigm

candidates.label: Merge sort algorithm

This approach is known as the merge sort algorithm.

candidates.label: Binary search
candidates.context: Binary search, a decrease-and-conquer algorithm where the subproblems are of roughly half the original size, has a long history.

candidates.label: Sorted list
candidates.context: The name "divide and conquer" is sometimes applied to algorithms that reduce each problem to only one sub-problem, such as the binary search algorithm for finding a record in a sorted list (or its analogue in numerical computing, the bisection algorithm for root finding).

candidates.context: The name decrease and conquer has been proposed instead for the single-subproblem class.

candidates.label: Prune
candidates.context: An important application of divide and conquer is in optimization, where if the search space is reduced ("pruned") by a constant factor at each step, the overall algorithm has the same asymptotic complexity as the pruning step, with the constant depending on the pruning factor (by summing the geometric series); this is known as prune and search.

definitions.1: A category of decision problems that are at least as hard as any other problem in the class NP, meaning a potential solution can be verified quickly.
definitions.2: A characterization of an algorithm whose execution time grows no faster than a polynomial function of the input size, often considered efficient for practical computational use.
definitions.3: An algorithmic approach that systematically checks every possible candidate solution to find the correct one, typically resulting in exponential time complexity for hard problems.
definitions.4: A set of decision problems for which a proposed solution can be verified as correct or incorrect within a time frame that is polynomial relative to the input size.
definitions.5: A theoretical model of computation where the machine can effectively exist in multiple states simultaneously, often used to define the class NP formally.
definitions.6: A procedure that solves a computational problem in time that is a polynomial function of the input size, allowing the problem to be considered computationally tractable.
definitions.12: The formal property of a decision problem belonging to the set NP while simultaneously being difficult enough that every other problem in NP can be reduced to it.
definitions.13: A category of problems that are at least as hard as the hardest problems in NP, but which do not necessarily belong to the class NP themselves.
definitions.14: A fundamental logic problem determining if there exists an assignment of truth values to variables that makes a given Boolean expression evaluate to true.
definitions.16: A standard method of transforming one problem into another such that if the second problem can be solved efficiently, the first can also be solved efficiently.
definitions.18: A category of graphs that can be drawn in a two-dimensional plane without any edges crossing, often allowing for more efficient algorithms for specific computational problems.
definitions.19: The problem of determining whether two graphs are structurally identical by identifying if there exists a mapping that preserves adjacency between vertices.

candidates.label: Transaction fails
candidates.context: Atomicity guarantees that each transaction is treated as a single "unit", which either succeeds completely or fails completely: if any of the statements constituting a transaction fails to complete, the entire transaction fails and the database is left unchanged.

candidates.label: Databases prioritize
candidates.context: ACID databases prioritize consistency over availability — the whole transaction fails if an error occurs in any step within the transaction; in contrast, BASE databases prioritize availability over consistency: instead of failing the transaction, users can access inconsistent data temporarily: data consistency is achieved, but not immediately.

candidates.label: NoSQL databases

candidates.label: Consistent state
candidates.context: Consistency ensures that a transaction can only bring the database from one consistent state to another, preserving database invariants: any data written to the database must be valid according to all defined rules, including constraints, cascades, triggers, and any combination thereof.

candidates.label: Database invariant

candidates.label: Atomic transaction

candidates.label: Series of operations
candidates.context: The series of operations cannot be separated with only some of them being executed, which makes the series of operations "indivisible".

candidates.label: Physical transactions
candidates.context: Unless and until all component physical transactions are executed, the logical transaction will not have occurred.

candidates.label: Write-ahead logging
candidates.context: In write ahead logging, durability is guaranteed by writing the prospective change to a persistent log before changing the database.

candidates.label: Locking
candidates.context: Locking means that the transaction marks the data that it accesses so that the DBMS knows not to allow other transactions to modify it until the first transaction succeeds or fails.

candidates.label: Two-phase locking

candidates.label: Reading transaction
candidates.context: An alternative to locking is multiversion concurrency control, in which the database provides each reading transaction the prior, unmodified version of data that is being modified by another active transaction.

candidates.label: Expanding phase
candidates.context: By the 2PL protocol, locks are applied and removed in two phases: Expanding phase: locks are acquired and no locks are released.

candidates.label: Shrinking phase
candidates.context: Shrinking phase: locks are released and no locks are acquired.

candidates.label: Basic protocol
candidates.context: Refinements of the basic protocol may use more lock types.

candidates.label: Exclusive locks
candidates.context: Two types of locks are used by the basic protocol: Shared and Exclusive locks.

candidates.label: S2PL
candidates.context: To comply with the strict two-phase locking (S2PL) protocol, a transaction needs to comply with 2PL, and release its write (exclusive) locks only after the transaction has ended (i.e., either committed or aborted).

candidates.label: Write-lock
candidates.context: For 2PL, the only used data-access locks are read-locks (shared locks) and write-locks (exclusive locks).

candidates.label: Read-lock
candidates.context: Below are the rules for read-locks and write-locks: A transaction is allowed to read an object if and only if it is holding a read-lock or write-lock on that object.

candidates.label: C2PL
candidates.context: Conservative two-phase locking (C2PL) differs from 2PL in that transactions obtain all the locks they need before the actual execution begins.

candidates.label: Lock contention
candidates.context: In cases of heavy lock contention, C2PL reduces the time locks are held on average, relative to 2PL and Strict 2PL, because transactions that hold locks are never blocked.

candidates.label: B-trees
candidates.context: Unlike 2PL, S2PL provides strictness (a special case of cascade-less recoverability). This protocol is not appropriate in B-trees because it causes Bottleneck (while B-trees always starts searching from the parent root).

candidates.context: Every SS2PL schedule is also an S2PL schedule, but not vice versa.

mcqs.q: If a database transaction has released a lock but currently needs to acquire a new one to proceed, what is the implication regarding the Two-Phase Locking protocol?
options: The transaction is in the shrinking phase and violates the 2PL protocol.
The transaction is permitted to acquire the lock if it upgrades to an exclusive lock.
The transaction is in the expanding phase, so it is allowed to continue.
The transaction must immediately restart to avoid deadlock.
mcqs.why: The defining rule of 2PL is that once a lock is released, no new locks can be acquired, meaning the transaction has entered the shrinking phase.

mcqs.q: What is the primary trade-off associated with Conservative Two-Phase Locking (C2PL) compared to standard 2PL?
options: It increases the probability of deadlocks in exchange for lower overhead.
It avoids deadlocks but often holds locks longer than necessary, increasing overhead.
It is faster because it allows transactions to acquire locks dynamically.
It provides better concurrency by allowing more transactions to run in parallel.
mcqs.why: C2PL prevents deadlocks by requiring all locks upfront, but this leads to inefficiency because it holds locks longer than necessary and requires predicting future lock needs.

mcqs.q: Why is a schedule following Strong Strict Two-Phase Locking (SS2PL) considered more restrictive than one following standard 2PL?
options: Because it requires transactions to release all locks before they commit.
Because it prevents any read-only transactions from executing.
Because it holds all locks until the end, whereas standard 2PL allows releasing read locks during the shrinking phase.
Because it forces transactions to execute serially rather than concurrently.
mcqs.why: Standard 2PL allows releasing read locks during the shrinking phase, while SS2PL keeps all locks (read and write) held until the transaction completely finishes.

mcqs.q: Which best describes the primary purpose of layering in the Internet protocol suite?
options: To increase the speed of physical data transmission
To allow protocols at different levels to operate independently through abstraction
To ensure every protocol can communicate with every hardware device
To eliminate the need for routers in network communication

mcqs.q: Why is a three-way handshake necessary for a TCP connection instead of a two-way exchange?

To maximize the speed of data transmission by pre-allocating bandwidth
To encrypt the data payload before transmission begins
To allow the server to reject clients that do not have an IP address

mcqs.q: How does TCP handle segments that arrive out of order at the destination?

mcqs.q: Why is the DNS described as a hierarchical and distributed system?
options: It stores all Internet data in one central location for fast access.
It delegates authority across multiple servers to avoid a single point of failure.
It uses a single database file shared by every ISP in the world.
It requires every device to hold a copy of the entire Internet directory.
mcqs.why: DNS avoids a central database by delegating authority, making it distributed and fault-tolerant.

mcqs.q: When is a glue record necessary in the DNS?
options: When the parent domain server cannot find the IP address of the child domain's name server.
When a user wants to cache the IP address of a website for faster browsing.
When a TLD server needs to define a new root server.
When the authoritative name server for a subdomain is itself located within that subdomain.
mcqs.why: Glue records are needed to resolve circular dependencies where the server address is inside the domain it serves.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes an authoritative name server from a non-authoritative (caching) server?
options: It provides answers derived directly from the master configuration of the zone.
It is always located at the root of the DNS tree structure.
It only handles requests from other authoritative name servers.
It stores the entire database of all IP addresses on the Internet.
mcqs.why: Authoritative servers serve data they own/manage, whereas others simply cache results.

mcqs.q: Why were many early programming languages designed to be compilable in a single pass?
options: To simplify the language grammar for beginners
To reduce the memory footprint and complexity of early compilers
To ensure the generated code was always faster than interpreted code
To make the compiler compatible with all hardware architectures
mcqs.why: Early computers had limited memory, so splitting the compiler into a single pass was a practical necessity.

mcqs.q: What is the primary purpose of the compiler's front end?
options: To generate machine code for the target CPU
To perform optimizations on the intermediate representation
To analyze the source code and produce an intermediate representation
To link object files into an executable program

mcqs.q: What is a key characteristic of the intermediate representation (IR) in a compiler?

It is an architecture-independent representation of the source program
It is used only for debugging the compiled program
It is a high-level abstract syntax tree
mcqs.why: The IR is a lower-level but still architecture-independent representation used for optimization.

mcqs.q: Why does k-means clustering minimize squared Euclidean distances rather than regular Euclidean distances?
options: Because the centroid is the point that minimizes the sum of squared distances to all points in the cluster.
Because regular Euclidean distance is not defined in high-dimensional spaces.
Because k-means was originally designed for signal compression, which only uses squared errors.
Because the geometric median is computationally too expensive to calculate for large datasets.
mcqs.why: The centroid is mathematically proven to minimize the sum of squared deviations.

mcqs.q: What is the primary reason Lloyd's algorithm is considered efficient in practice despite the k-means problem being NP-hard?
options: It guarantees finding the global optimum in polynomial time for all datasets.
It converges to a local optimum very quickly, often in a small number of iterations.
It avoids the NP-hard nature by only working on two-dimensional data.
It uses the Forgy initialization method, which is always optimal.
mcqs.why: The text states it converges quickly to a local optimum, making it practical.

mcqs.q: If the total variance of a dataset is constant, what does minimizing the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) imply about the Between-Cluster Sum of Squares (BCSS)?
options: BCSS must also decrease to maintain the constant total variance.
BCSS must increase because the two components are inversely related.
BCSS remains unchanged as it is independent of WCSS.
BCSS becomes zero, indicating all clusters are identical.

mcqs.q: Why is cross-validation generally preferred over a single holdout method for assessing model performance?
options: It requires less computational power than a single holdout split.
It uses all data points for both training and validation across iterations, providing a more stable estimate.
It completely eliminates the possibility of overfitting during model training.
It only requires a single split of the data into training and test sets.
mcqs.why: The key advantage is that every data point is used for validation exactly once, smoothing out performance estimates.

mcqs.q: In leave-one-out cross-validation, what happens to the training set for each iteration?
options: The entire dataset is used for both training and validation.
One observation is removed, and the remaining n-1 observations are used for training.
The data is split into k equal folds, with one fold used for training.
The validation set is larger than the training set in each iteration.
mcqs.why: By definition, LOOCV iteratively leaves out exactly one observation for validation.

mcqs.q: What is a primary limitation of using only the holdout method for model evaluation?
options: It requires the model to be trained on the entire dataset before evaluation.
The evaluation results can be highly variable and unstable due to a single random split.
It cannot be used for classification tasks, only regression.
It always results in an optimistic bias for the model's performance.
mcqs.why: The article explicitly warns that the single run of the holdout method can yield misleading, unstable results.

definitions.1: A multilayer perceptron is a feedforward neural network with fully connected layers and nonlinear activation functions, used for tasks like classification.
definitions.2: A feedforward neural network is an architecture where information flows unidirectionally from input to output without any cycles or feedback loops.
definitions.3: A multilayer perceptron is a modern feedforward neural network consisting of fully connected neurons with nonlinear activation functions organized in layers.
definitions.4: A neural network is a broad computational model inspired by biological networks, encompassing various architectures like feedforward and recurrent types.
definitions.5: A nonlinear activation function is a mathematical function applied to a neuron's weighted sum to introduce nonlinearity, enabling the network to learn complex patterns.
definitions.6: Fully connected describes a network topology where every neuron in one layer is directly connected to every neuron in the next layer.
definitions.7: Deep learning is a subfield of machine learning using multi-layered neural networks to automatically learn hierarchical representations of data.
definitions.8: Fully connected neurons are artificial neurons in a layer that receive inputs from every neuron in the preceding layer via learnable weights.
definitions.9: Vanilla networks are colloquial terms for standard, non-specialized neural network architectures like basic multilayer perceptrons without advanced modifications.
definitions.10: A rectified linear unit is a common piecewise linear activation function that outputs zero for negative inputs and the input value for positive inputs.
definitions.11: A hidden layer is a computational layer in a neural network between the input and output layers whose values are not directly observed in the training data.
definitions.12: Deep feedforward networks are multilayer perceptrons with multiple hidden layers that can learn hierarchical representations of input data.
definitions.14: A layer connection refers to the complete set of weighted links between every neuron in one layer and every neuron in the immediately following layer.
definitions.15: An output layer is the final layer of a neural network that produces the network's prediction, with its structure and activation depending on the task.
definitions.16: An input layer is the first layer of a neural network that receives the initial data signal, such as image pixels or feature vectors.
definitions.18: Stochastic gradient descent is an optimization algorithm that iteratively updates network weights by computing gradients on small random batches of data.
definitions.20: A deep MLP is a multilayer perceptron with many hidden layers, enabling it to learn hierarchical representations of data.
definitions.23: A weighted sum is the linear combination of a neuron's inputs, where each input is multiplied by its corresponding synaptic weight.
definitions.24: Input connections are the synaptic links from previous layer neurons to a given neuron, each associated with a learnable weight representing connection strength.
definitions.25: Learnable parameters are the adjustable weights and biases in a neural network that are updated during training to minimize a loss function.
definitions.26: A linear activation function is a function that outputs the weighted sum directly, which reduces a multilayer network to an equivalent single layer.
definitions.30: A two-layer input-output model is the simplified equivalent of a multilayer perceptron where all layers collapse into a single linear transformation.
definitions.31: Biological neurons are the natural, living cells that process electrical signals, serving as the conceptual inspiration for artificial neural network units.
definitions.32: A function that maps inputs is a mathematical operation, like an activation function, that transforms the weighted sum of neuron inputs into an output value.
definitions.33: The vanishing gradient problem is a challenge in training deep networks where gradients become extremely small as they are backpropagated through many layers.
definitions.37: An output node is a single neuron in the output layer that produces one component of the network's final prediction.
definitions.39: Layer weights are the learnable parameters connecting neurons between consecutive layers, which are adjusted during the network's training process.
definitions.40: A loss function is a mathematical measure of the difference between a network's predicted outputs and the actual target values, used to guide training.
definitions.41: A forward pass is the process of computing a network's output by propagating input data through each layer in a single direction.
definitions.42: A backward pass is the process of computing gradients of the loss function with respect to the network's parameters using backpropagation.

mcqs.q: Why is the fully connected topology of an MLP less practical for high-dimensional inputs like images?
options: It cannot process image data at all.
The number of parameters grows quadratically, leading to high memory and computational costs.
It requires a linear activation function.
It prevents the use of nonlinear activation functions.
mcqs.why: The quadratic scaling of parameters in fully connected layers makes them inefficient for large input dimensions.

mcqs.q: What is the primary reason MLPs require nonlinear activation functions instead of linear ones?
options: Linear functions are too slow to compute.
Linear functions cause the network to collapse into a two-layer model, losing representational power.
They are required for the backpropagation algorithm to work.
They are easier to implement than linear functions.
mcqs.why: Without nonlinearity, multiple layers become mathematically equivalent to a single linear transformation.

mcqs.q: Why are the internal layers of an MLP referred to as 'hidden'?
options: They are not used during the forward pass.
Their values are not directly observed in the training data, unlike inputs and outputs.
They are located between the input and output layers.
They only use linear activation functions.
mcqs.why: The term 'hidden' specifically refers to the fact that the activations of these layers are not directly available in the dataset.

mcqs.q: Why is the 'Dying ReLU' problem considered a significant issue in training deep neural networks?
options: It causes the output to explode to infinity
It makes the network non-differentiable at all points
It results in neurons that stop outputting non-zero values, blocking all gradient flow
It forces the network to become zero-centered unnecessarily
mcqs.why: Dying ReLU renders neurons permanently inactive, effectively removing them from the learning process.

mcqs.q: What is the primary advantage of using smooth approximations like Softplus or GELU over the standard ReLU?
options: They are computationally cheaper to calculate than ReLU
They provide continuous derivatives, which can lead to more stable gradient descent
They force the network to become linear
They prevent the vanishing gradient problem entirely by using sigmoid functions
mcqs.why: Smooth functions allow for continuous gradients everywhere, unlike ReLU which has a discontinuity in the derivative at zero.

mcqs.q: If a ReLU activation function is scale-invariant, what does this imply about the network's parameters?
options: The network can compute the same output even if weights and biases are scaled proportionally
The network's learning rate must be adjusted based on the input scale
The weights must always be positive
The output is always bounded between 0 and 1
mcqs.why: Scale-invariance means the function remains identical under proportional scaling, allowing for equivalent computation with different weight magnitudes.

definitions.1: A machine learning paradigm where models use the data itself to generate supervisory signals instead of relying on external labels.

definitions.3: A signal derived from inherent data structures or relationships that is used to train a model without manual annotation.
definitions.4: The raw material fed into a model, which in SSL is transformed to create related sample pairs for generating supervisory signals.

definitions.6: A machine learning approach that discovers inherent structures in data without using any external labels or supervisory signals.
definitions.8: Data points that lack explicit, human-provided labels and are used as raw input for unsupervised or self-supervised training.
definitions.10: A compressed, lower-dimensional representation of the input data learned by an autoencoder's encoder network.

definitions.14: A statistical method to optimize models by maximizing the agreement between positive sample pairs while using negative examples.
definitions.15: Architectures like Barlow Twins and VICReg that learn invariant representations by enforcing covariance constraints between data views.
definitions.16: A multimodal approach that generalizes joint-embedding by using path models to enforce correlation across different data types.
definitions.17: A framework by Yann LeCun that learns a world model in latent space to enable reasoning and autonomous intelligence in machines.

mcqs.q: What is the primary mechanism by which self-supervised learning generates supervisory signals?
options: By using manually annotated labels from human experts.
By transforming the input data into related pairs where one serves as a target for the other.
By randomly assigning labels to each data point in the dataset.
By using a separate labeled dataset to initialize the model parameters.
mcqs.why: SSL creates pseudo-labels by transforming input data into related pairs, using one as a target for the other.

mcqs.q: How does the loss function in contrastive learning operate?
options: It minimizes the distance between positive sample pairs and maximizes it between negative pairs.
It minimizes the distance between all samples, regardless of their labels.
It only maximizes the distance between positive pairs to separate them.
It does not use a loss function and instead relies on direct reconstruction.
mcqs.why: The core principle of contrastive learning is to bring positive pairs closer and push negative pairs apart.

mcqs.q: What is a key feature of JEPA that distinguishes it from autoencoders?
options: JEPA operates entirely in the latent space to learn a world model.
JEPA requires labeled data to initialize the model parameters.
JEPA only reconstructs the original input data without any prediction.
JEPA uses a single network instead of an encoder-decoder architecture.
mcqs.why: Unlike autoencoders that reconstruct input, JEPA learns in latent space to build a predictive world model.

mcqs.q: Why is message passing a key design element in GNNs for molecular drug design?

mcqs.q: What is the primary advantage of using multi-head attention in a GAT layer?

mcqs.q: What phenomenon in deep GNNs is characterized by node representations converging to a uniform value?

candidates.label: Fine-tuning
candidates.context: Fine-tuning involves applying additional training (e.g., on new data) to the parameters of a neural network that have been pre-trained.

candidates.label: Pre-trained
candidates.context: Models that are pre-trained on large, general corpora are usually fine-tuned by reusing their parameters as a starting point and adding a task-specific layer trained from scratch.

candidates.label: Neural network
candidates.context: For some architectures, such as convolutional neural networks, it is common to keep the earlier layers (those closest to the input layer) frozen, as they capture lower-level features, while later layers often discern high-level features that can be more related to the task that the model is trained on.

candidates.label: Fine-tuned
candidates.context: A model may also be augmented with "adapters"—lightweight modules inserted into the model's architecture that nudge the embedding space for domain adaptation. These contain far fewer parameters than the original model and can be fine-tuned in a parameter-efficient way by tuning only their weights and leaving the rest of the model's weights frozen.

candidates.label: Language model
candidates.context: Commercially-offered large language models can sometimes be fine-tuned if the provider offers a fine-tuning API.

candidates.label: Fine-tuned model
candidates.context: One mitigation is to linearly interpolate a fine-tuned model's weights with the weights of the original model, which can greatly increase out-of-distribution performance while largely retaining the in-distribution performance of the fine-tuned model.

candidates.label: Low-rank
candidates.context: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is an adapter-based technique for efficiently fine-tuning models.

candidates.label: Hugging Face
candidates.context: Support for LoRA was integrated into the diffusers library from Hugging Face.

candidates.label: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)
candidates.context: Support for LoRA and similar techniques is also available for a wide range of other models through Hugging Face's parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) package.

candidates.label: Large language models (LLMs)
candidates.context: Representation fine-tuning (ReFT) is a technique developed by researchers at Stanford University aimed at fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) by modifying less than 1% of their representations.

candidates.label: Pre-trained model
candidates.context: Large language models like OpenAI's series of GPT foundation models can be fine-tuned on data for specific downstream NLP tasks (tasks that use a pre-trained model) to improve performance over the unmodified pre-trained model.

candidates.label: Entities
candidates.context: Platforms such as Semrush's AI Visibility Toolkit and Enterprise AIO exemplify how fine-tuned models are being used for entity-level monitoring; tracking how named entities are referenced and represented within responses generated by large-language-model-based answer engines.

To make the algorithm behave like depth-first search

The cost function will be linear with respect to path length

mcqs.q: Why does alpha-beta pruning effectively reduce the search time in a minimax tree?
options: It eliminates branches that cannot possibly influence the final decision.
It evaluates nodes in a random order to find cutoffs faster.
It reduces the branching factor by half at every node.
It only searches the first half of the tree depth.

definitions.1: Natural language processing is the subfield of computer science and artificial intelligence focused on processing and understanding human language using computational methods.
definitions.2: Speech recognition is the computational task of converting a sound clip of spoken language into its corresponding textual representation.
definitions.3: Natural language understanding is a major NLP processing task focused on interpreting the meaning and structure of human language input.
definitions.4: The Turing test is a criterion for intelligence that evaluates a machine's ability to exhibit human-like natural language interpretation and generation.
definitions.5: Symbolic NLP is an early NLP approach that relies on explicitly coded rules and dictionaries to manipulate linguistic symbols and process text.
definitions.6: Machine translation is the automated task of translating text from one language into another, a major focus of early and statistical NLP research.
definitions.7: Statistical NLP is an approach that uses machine learning algorithms and probabilistic models trained on large text corpora instead of hand-written rules.
definitions.8: Statistical machine translation is a specific method that applies statistical models, such as IBM alignment models, to translate text based on probability.
definitions.9: ELIZA is a notable early symbolic NLP system from the 1960s that simulated conversation using simple pattern matching and substitution rules.
definitions.12: Rule-based systems are NLP architectures that operate by applying a predefined set of hand-coded rules and heuristics to process language.
definitions.13: Machine learning is a broad field of artificial intelligence that develops algorithms allowing computers to learn patterns from data without explicit programming.
definitions.14: Learning algorithms are computational procedures used to train models by finding optimal parameters from a dataset of examples or features.
definitions.15: Statistical NLP refers to the application of statistical methods and machine learning techniques to analyze and process human language.
definitions.16: IBM Research is an organization where significant early successes in statistical machine translation, including probabilistic alignment models, were developed in the 1990s.
definitions.17: Non-annotated data refers to raw text collections used in statistical NLP that do not contain manually labeled or marked-up linguistic information.

definitions.1: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) is the technology that translates spoken language into text or other interpretable forms.
definitions.2: Speech-to-text (STT) is an alternative term for the process of converting spoken words into written text.
definitions.3: Speech recognition is the computational sub-field concerned with methods and technologies that translate spoken language into text.
definitions.5: Deep learning refers to advances in neural network architectures that have accelerated progress in speech recognition systems.
definitions.6: Bell Labs is the research institution where foundational speech recognition systems like Audrey and Tangora were developed.
definitions.7: Dynamic time warping (DTW) is an algorithm used to measure similarity between sequences that may vary in speed or time.
definitions.9: Carnegie Mellon (CMU) is a university that participated in early speech recognition projects and developed the Sphinx system.
definitions.13: Language model is a method used to predict the probability distribution of a sequence of words in speech recognition.
definitions.14: Global Autonomous Language Exploitation (GALE) is a DARPA program focused on speech recognition for Arabic and Mandarin.
definitions.15: Artificial neural network (ANN) is a computational model inspired by biological neural networks, used for pattern recognition tasks.
definitions.16: Recurrent neural network (RNN) is a neural network architecture designed to recognize patterns in sequences of data.
definitions.17: Long short-term memory (LSTM) is a specialized type of recurrent neural network that can learn long-term dependencies.
definitions.18: Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) is an algorithm that allows training of recurrent neural networks for sequence labeling.
definitions.19: Language modelling is the statistical process of predicting the likelihood of a sequence of words in a given language.
definitions.21: Gaussian mixture model hidden Markov model is a hybrid model that uses GMMs to estimate observation probabilities in HMMs.
definitions.22: Vocal tract length normalization (VTLN) is a technique to normalize speaker vocal tract characteristics for recognition.
definitions.23: Maximum likelihood linear regression (MLLR) is an adaptation technique that transforms acoustic features to match a speaker.
definitions.25: Heteroscedastic linear discriminant analysis is a classification method used to model speaker-dependent acoustic variations.
definitions.26: Minimum classification error (MCE) is an optimization criterion that minimizes the classification error rate in speech recognition.
definitions.28: Maximum mutual information (MMI) is a discriminative training criterion that maximizes the mutual information between inputs and outputs.
definitions.29: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are neural networks with multiple hidden layers used to model complex acoustic patterns.
definitions.30: End-to-end is an approach where a single neural network directly maps input speech to output text without separate modules.
definitions.33: Word error rate (WER) is a metric that measures the percentage of words that are incorrectly recognized in speech recognition.
definitions.36: Listen Attend and Spell (LAS) is an end-to-end model that uses attention to map audio directly to text sequences.
definitions.40: Deep feedforward is a type of neural network where information flows in one direction from input to output layers.
